U.S. jury convicts Huawei in a criminal trial over fraud and trade secrets
sources.text:
Chinese technology giant Huawei was convicted Tuesday in New York on multiple federal criminal charges, including fraud, U.S. sanctions violations and conspiracy to steal trade secrets, following a three-month trial, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.
The verdict marks a major development in a long-running criminal case against Huawei, with charges first publicly disclosed in 2019.
A federal jury found Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty of multiple offenses, including bank and wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, the Justice Department said in a statement.
"No person or company is above the law," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said, accusing Huawei and its subsidiaries of conducting business in the United States through deception and theft.
The Justice Department said Huawei misrepresented its activities in Iran to banks to secure billions of dollars and retain access to U.S. dollar-clearing services. The company also supplied surveillance cameras that enabled Iranian authorities to monitor protests, the department said.
Among the examples of intellectual property theft detailed by prosecutors were cases involving Cisco and T-Mobile.
Huawei copied source code used in Cisco routers, with its engineers referring to Cisco by spelling its name backward in an attempt to conceal the theft.
Huawei employees also sent photographs and technical details of T-Mobile's touchscreen-testing robot to China, with one employee later removing a component from T-Mobile's laboratory in a backpack, according to the Justice Department.
"For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception," said Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division.
Huawei pushed back against the verdict in a statement issued Wednesday, while welcoming its acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge.
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," Huawei said, adding that the five trade secret-related disputes cited by prosecutors had previously been resolved as civil matters.
The company said it would review the verdicts and take necessary legal action to defend its interests, while remaining focused on maintaining uninterrupted business operations and investing in research and development.
Huawei and its subsidiaries face potential financial penalties, including fines, forfeiture and restitution, with sentencing scheduled for Sept. 14, 2027, according to the Justice Department.
U.S. prosecutors first publicly disclosed criminal charges against Huawei in January 2019, a month after the company's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, was arrested in Canada.
Meng returned to China in September 2021 after entering into a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. prosecutors.

sources.news_title: Huawei convicted of stealing trade secrets: What’s the case, and what does it mean for US-China ties? Explained
sources.text:
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies Co of stealing trade secrets Tuesday, but acquitted it of a more serious racketeering allegation, according to the Department of Justice.
Huawei Technologies Co, China’s largest technology company, was found guilty of multiple US criminal charges, including defrauding banks about its business in Iran and money laundering, Bloomberg reported.
A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, deliberated for about four days before reaching a verdict Tuesday in a rare US prosecution of a foreign corporation.
Jurors found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced — including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and conspiracy to defraud the United States, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) said.
The company was cleared of two charges, including racketeering and obstruction of justice, the report added.
"No person or company is above the law," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft,” he added.
The equipment manufacturer was accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process, news agency AFP reported.
That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to its competitors' and sell them at lower prices, according to the original indictment.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the DOJ said in a release.
Huawei even launched an internal programme offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors claimed.
The investigation also involved Huawei's business dealings with the government of Iran.
"Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community," DOJ said.
The jury ultimately acquitted the company of a racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice.
"Today's verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead," Assistant Attorney General Tysen A Duva said in a statement.
Huawei now faces potential fines, forfeiture and restitution, but the US has not specified the scope of financial penalties it will seek.
The world's leading telecom equipment manufacturer, Huawei, has been targeted by the Trump administration, which alleges that it poses a risk of spying on behalf of the Chinese government.
The United States previously urged countries not to use Huawei infrastructure for the rollout of new 5G mobile networks.
For most of that time, the company has been largely excluded from the American market under trade measures imposed by the Trump and Biden administrations in the name of national security, Bloomberg reported.
The telecom titan has emerged as China’s de facto national chipmaking champion and is one of a handful of firms central to Beijing’s goal of dominating artificial intelligence and replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents.
The verdict against one of China’s biggest and best-known tech giants lands at a delicate time for US-China relations. According to Bloomberg, it threatens to strain ties already frayed over revelations that the now-reinstated chief executive of Nvidia Corp, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.
Besides, the conviction is a vindication for the Justice Department, which overcame attempts by Huawei to derail the case before trial and had to navigate years of delays because of the Covid pandemic, which made it difficult for lawyers and witnesses to travel.
Along the way, two Chinese intelligence officers were accused in 2022 of trying to bribe a US law enforcement official with $61,000 in Bitcoin to steal evidence and get inside information about the case.
From the beginning, the Huawei case heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing while the world’s two largest economies were mired in a trade war.
Months later, officials in Trump’s administration labelled the company a national security threat, alleging that it sold telecommunications equipment that China’s Communist Party could use for spying.
The initial criminal indictment set off a diplomatic crisis when Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, whose father founded the company, was arrested at the US's behest on financial fraud charges while travelling through Canada.
Almost three years after Meng was held under house arrest in Vancouver, she reached a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021 that allowed her to return to China, but only after she admitted that the company violated US sanctions by illegally conducting business in Iran.
(With inputs from Bloomberg, AFP)

China's Huawei Convicted of Federal Racketeering, Evading Iran Sanctions, and Corporate Espionage.
sources.text:
A federal jury in New York has convicted Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei and three subsidiaries following a three-month criminal trial, finding the firms guilty of secretly aiding Iran’s regime, defrauding American financial institutions, laundering money, and systematically stealing trade secrets from American tech companies.
Returned in the Eastern District of New York on Tuesday, the verdicts cover Huawei’s parent company, Chinese affiliate Huawei Device Co. Ltd., and American units Futurewei Technologies Inc. and Huawei Device USA Inc. Federal prosecutors demonstrated that the defendants ran a decades-long criminal enterprise aimed at expanding Huawei’s global telecommunications footprint through fraud and corporate theft.
“No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche stated following the verdict. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft. Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable.”
National Security Threat.
Justice Department Criminal Division chief Tysen A. Duva declared that Huawei “built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” adding: “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security. Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead.”
Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor echoed that warning, stating Huawei “violated our laws, empowered our enemies, and harmed our national security,” while Eastern District of New York U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. noted the convictions mark “a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”
FBI Counterintelligence and Espionage Division Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky added that the outcome serves as “a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security,” proving that “no company is too big, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the U.S. and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”
Secretly Building Iran’s Surveillance State and Lying to Banks.
Trial evidence revealed that Huawei and its affiliates supplied Tehran with turnkey infrastructure to expand mobile networks and build an internet backbone across the Islamic Republic. Huawei also partnered with Iranian regime officials and Zaeim—an arm of Iran’s intelligence apparatus—to monitor and censor internet traffic, while providing surveillance cameras used by Tehran to track domestic protesters.
Operating inside Iran through a covert subsidiary named “Skycom,” Huawei repeatedly misled journalists, American officials, and major banks, falsely claiming it had curtailed Iranian operations in 2011, had never aided Tehran’s military or intelligence services, complied fully with U.S. sanctions, and merely partnered with Skycom rather than owning it outright. Relying on those misrepresentations, Huawei secured billions of dollars in financing alongside access to U.S.-dollar clearing channels essential to competing internationally.
Decades of Industrial Espionage Against American Firms.
Alongside sanctions evasion, Huawei ran a sustained conspiracy to pilfer proprietary designs, source code, and manuals from American competitors and business partners. At T-Mobile, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement with the deliberate intent to break it, photographing and measuring T-Mobile’s touchscreen-testing robot, “Tappy,” before a Huawei staffer smuggled a robotic component out of T-Mobile’s restricted lab inside a backpack.
To replicate Cisco router software, regarded as the “crown jewel” of Cisco’s engineering, Huawei programmers lifted proprietary code and clumsily attempted to scrub their tracks by spelling Cisco backward as “ocsic” inside the surviving developer notes. In another scheme, a Huawei operative caught snapping photos of restricted Fujitsu hardware wore a counterfeit badge identifying his employer as “Weihua.”
When U.S. firm CNEX refused to partner directly with the Chinese giant, Huawei recruited a university academic to enter a research arrangement with CNEX without disclosing his Huawei backing, funneling confidential data and direct access to CNEX’s proprietary hardware back to China. Similarly, after obtaining confidential antenna designs from American manufacturer Quintel under a non-disclosure agreement, Huawei promptly filed its own patent application incorporating Quintel’s technology, even attaching a confidential slide Quintel had shared.
Jurors convicted Huawei and its three subsidiaries on multiple counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, money laundering conspiracy, and both substantive and conspiracy violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
The companies face steep criminal fines, asset forfeiture, and restitution when sentenced on September 14, 2027.

US jury convicts Huawei of violating sanctions, stealing trade secrets
November 25, 2026
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei on a slew of charges on Tuesday including stealing trade secrets and violating sanctions.
The jury in the Brooklyn federal court found the company guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts that it faced, which also included bank fraud and wire fraud.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said after the verdict.
However, the jury acquitted Huawei on two charges of racketeering and conspiring to obstruct justice.
The verdict is the latest blow to the Chinese tech giant which has for years been banned from selling networking devices to telecom carries in the US and other Western countries. However, its consumer electronics business has continued to grow as its networking business in other countries.
Stolen source code, antenna technology and robot tech
Prosecutors detailed a number of ways Huawei stole trade secrets from competitors in order to undercut them in the market.
In once instance, a Huawei employee slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade fair in order to photograph circuitboards inside another company's networking divice.
Huawei was also found to have once sold routers containing source code from a rival company.
Prosecutors also said a Huawei employee once removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
According to court records, the victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the Department of Justice said.
False statenments about Iran operations
Prosecutors also alleged that Huawei did business in countries subject to US sanctions including Iran and North Korea.
Huawei then made false statements to both US government officials and banks in order to hide this activity, prosecutors said.
"Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the ‌enforcement of US laws," US Attorney Joseph Nocella said.
Huawei to appeal verdict
Huawei continued to deny the allegations even after the verdict on Tuesday.
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company said in a statement.
"The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation."
The company's lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said: "We fully expect to appeal."
Huawei is set to be sentenced next September and could face billions of dollars in penalties.

sources.news_title: China's Huawei convicted in US in sprawling criminal trial over Iran business
sources.text:
Huawei was found guilty by a federal jury in Brooklyn on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced. It was found not guilty of racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company acted as a criminal enterprise.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has nonetheless not undermined Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial.
"After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during her closing argument.
FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER HAD BEEN DETAINED
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
PROSECUTORS ALLEGED TRADE SECRETS THEFT
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC , Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel's antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
DEFENSE SAYS BANKS KNEW OF IRAN BUSINESS
The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for Huawei's business.
Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development."
The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

sources.news_title: Huawei Found Guilty of Stealing Trade Secrets in Major US Criminal Trial
sources.text:
Huawei has been found guilty of stealing trade secrets, committing bank fraud and violating US sanctions following a lengthy criminal trial in New York. A federal jury convicted the Chinese technology giant on 10 of 12 criminal counts, bringing a major development in a case that has been unfolding for years.
The verdict, delivered on 24 November 2026, also covers three Huawei subsidiaries. Prosecutors accused the company of running a decades-long operation involving the theft of intellectual property from American technology businesses, concealing its activities in Iran and misleading financial institutions to maintain access to international banking services.
However, the jury also rejected two of the most serious allegations, acquitting Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.
Huawei has said it intends to appeal the convictions.
What Was Huawei Found Guilty Of?
The case involved several different allegations, including trade secret theft, wire fraud, bank fraud, money laundering and violations of US sanctions.
Prosecutors argued that Huawei and its subsidiaries repeatedly obtained confidential technology from American businesses, sometimes through business partnerships and non-disclosure agreements that were allegedly used to gain access to proprietary information.
The companies involved included T-Mobile, Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, Fujitsu, Quintel USA and semiconductor company CNEX.
Among the examples presented to the jury were:
- T-Mobile’s Tappy robot: Huawei employees were accused of taking photographs and technical information about T-Mobile’s robotic testing equipment. One employee allegedly removed a component from the robot inside a controlled laboratory and carried it out in a backpack.
- Cisco router technology: Prosecutors said Huawei copied proprietary source code used in Cisco networking equipment. Investigators also presented evidence that Huawei engineers had retained Cisco’s original comments and references within copied code.
- Quintel antenna technology: Huawei was accused of obtaining confidential antenna designs under a non-disclosure agreement before incorporating elements of the technology into a patent application.
- CNEX semiconductor technology: Prosecutors alleged that Huawei used an intermediary to gain access to confidential hardware and information belonging to the US semiconductor company.
- Fujitsu equipment: A Huawei employee was accused of photographing proprietary equipment at a trade show while using a badge identifying himself as an employee of another company.
These examples formed part of the prosecution’s broader argument that Huawei had systematically targeted competitors and business partners to obtain technology.
The Iran Connection and Misleading Banks
The trial also examined Huawei’s business dealings in Iran and how the company allegedly concealed those activities from international banks.
According to prosecutors, Huawei conducted business in Iran through a company called Skycom, which they said was effectively a wholly owned subsidiary rather than an independent business partner.
The US government argued that Huawei misrepresented its relationship with Skycom and the extent of its Iranian operations to banks, including HSBC. Those representations allegedly allowed Huawei to maintain access to US-dollar financial services despite restrictions on doing business with Iran.
Prosecutors also presented evidence that Huawei provided telecommunications infrastructure and surveillance technology to Iranian authorities. This included equipment that could be used to monitor and censor internet access, as well as surveillance cameras used to monitor protest activity.
The jury ultimately found Huawei guilty of offences involving sanctions violations, bank and wire fraud, and money laundering, alongside the trade secret conspiracy.
The Case Dates Back to 2018
The criminal proceedings have their origins in 2018, when Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, was arrested in Canada following a US extradition request.
Meng, the daughter of Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei, was accused of misleading HSBC about the company’s business relationship with Skycom and its activities in Iran.
She spent almost three years fighting extradition before reaching a deferred prosecution agreement with US authorities in 2021. She returned to China, and the charges against her were subsequently dismissed.
The wider case against Huawei continued, with US prosecutors expanding their allegations to include a long-running conspiracy to steal trade secrets from American technology companies.
The trial itself lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling over 60 witnesses and the defence presenting 15.
Huawei Plans to Appeal
Huawei has rejected the allegations and criticised the prosecution’s case.
The company argued that prosecutors had taken isolated incidents involving individual employees and presented them as evidence of a wider corporate conspiracy. Its lawyers also maintained that some of the technology in question was publicly available or had been addressed through previous licensing agreements and compliance measures.
Huawei’s defence described the verdict as legally flawed and confirmed that the company intends to pursue an appeal.
The jury’s decision to acquit Huawei on racketeering conspiracy and obstruction-related charges is also significant. It means the company was not found guilty of every allegation brought against it, despite the convictions on the remaining counts.
What Happens Next?
Huawei and its three subsidiaries are scheduled to be sentenced on 14 September 2027.
The penalties could include substantial criminal fines, forfeiture of assets and restitution to affected companies. The final sentence will be determined by a federal judge after considering the relevant sentencing guidelines and other legal factors.
The verdict also arrives years after the US placed Huawei on its trade blacklist in 2019, restricting its access to American technology and suppliers over national security concerns.
Despite those restrictions, Huawei has continued operating internationally and expanded its business across smartphones, telecommunications infrastructure, cloud services and semiconductor development.
Whether this latest conviction will significantly affect its global operations remains to be seen. For now, the verdict represents a major legal setback for one of the world’s largest technology companies, while Huawei’s planned appeal means the case is far from over.

sources.news_title: Huawei's 2013 Bonus Scheme: US Prosecutors Say Employees Were Paid for Rivals' Confidential Information
sources.text:
Huawei's 2013 Bonus Scheme: US Prosecutors Say Employees Were Paid for Rivals' Confidential Information
Prosecutors cited a 2013 policy offering payments for competitors' confidential information as a Brooklyn jury convicted Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets
Huawei was convicted by a federal jury in Brooklyn on 24 November of conspiring to steal trade secrets from rival companies. Prosecutors had presented a 2013 policy that they said offered employees payments for obtaining competitors' confidential information.
The jury found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy to violate US sanctions and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. It acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.
Prosecutors presented the bonus policy as evidence of a wider effort to obtain competitors' technology over roughly two decades. The trade-secret conspiracy conviction did not amount to separate findings on every incident cited by the government.
A 2013 Policy Set Payments for Confidential Information
A third superseding indictment filed in the Eastern District of New York on 13 February 2020 described a policy Huawei introduced in July 2013. It said the company established a rewards schedule for employees of Huawei affiliates who obtained confidential information from competitors, with payments based on the value of the material.
Under the policy described in the indictment, employees were instructed to upload information to an internal Huawei website or send especially sensitive material through encrypted email to a designated company mailbox. A 'competition management group' reviewed submissions and awarded monthly bonuses to employees who provided the most valuable information. The top regional divisions could also receive twice-yearly awards.
A separate indictment filed in January 2019 in the Western District of Washington specified that the top three regions could receive those awards. It also described a 12 July 2013 email from Huawei USA's Executive Director of Human Resources to US employees. The indictment said the email stated that collecting competitors' confidential information was prohibited under Huawei USA policy, while acknowledging that such a programme might be considered normal in some other countries and regions. It did not say that Huawei China's bonus programme had been suspended.
Prosecutors Cited Incidents Involving Rival Companies

sources.text:
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy to steal intellectual property from American companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn’t actually exist.
It’s unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
That hasn’t stopped the company from doing a robust business elsewhere. Its smartphones and other telecom equipment are sold globally. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors, becoming an important alternative in China to chips made by companies such as Nvidia.
The US announced its criminal charges against Huawei in early 2019 and later expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the US has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.
The indictment against Huawei accused it of a long pattern of outright technology theft. Huawei, prosecutors said, once sold internet routers containing source code copied from a competitor. In another episode, a person working for Huawei slipped into a competitor’s booth at a Chicago trade show to surreptitiously photograph the circuits inside another company’s networking device, the indictment said. Prosecutors said that on another occasion, a Huawei worker removed a robotic arm from a competitor’s lab so it could be photographed and measured.
The victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to court records.
“The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating US sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury at the trial.
In his closing argument to jurors, Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said prosecutors leaned on “innuendo and facts ripped out of context,” and testimony from ex-employees “with a bone to pick,” to pursue a company that had relied on “hard work, innovation and competition” to succeed.
“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” Heberlig said, noting that much of the material the US alleges was stolen was already public.
“You can’t steal a secret that isn’t a secret,” he said.
He said Huawei paid billions of dollars in licensing fees over the years, with 75% of that money going to US companies, and had reprimanded or fired employees found to have engaged in wrongdoing.
Heberlig noted that lines of Cisco source code turned up in Huawei software more than two decades ago. He said when the source-code copying was discovered, Huawei recalled routers sold in the US and offered to replace them with Cisco routers and created a “compliance culture that permeates Huawei today.”
US prosecutors had originally also brought criminal charges against Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, accusing her of misleading HSBC bank about the company’s business dealings in Iran. Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, was arrested in Canada in 2018, but ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the US dropped its case against Meng.

New York jury convicts Huawei of stealing trade secrets
A New York jury has found Chinese telecom giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and other criminal offences, but acquitted it of a racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. The verdict followed a three-month trial in New York in a case that adds to longstanding US efforts to curb Huawei's operations over alleged threats to national security.
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei of stealing trade secrets Tuesday, but acquitted it of a more serious racketeering allegation, according to the Department of Justice.
The world's leading telecom equipment manufacturer, Huawei has been targeted by the Trump administration, which alleges a risk of it spying on behalf of the Chinese government.
The United States has previously urged countries not to use Huawei infrastructure for the rollout of new 5G mobile networks.
The verdict followed a three-month trial at a New York federal court, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) reported, with jurors finding Huawei guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts facing it -- including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the United States.
"No person or company is above the law," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft."
'Necessary legal actions'
The jury did, however, acquit the company of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice, a move Huawei said in a statement it "welcomed," adding that it "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years."
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit... We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests," the statement continued.
The charges in part involved Huawei's business dealings with the government of Iran.
"Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community," DOJ said.
"Huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of US dollars and access to US-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services -- in part because of its lies."
The equipment manufacturer was also accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process.
That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to those of its competitors, which it then sold at lower prices, according to the original indictment.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the DOJ said in a release.
Huawei even launched an internal program offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors claimed.
"Today's verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead," Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement.

The case’s best-known defendant never saw a jury. She went home to China in 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement, in a swap that freed two Canadians Beijing had detained, and the US dropped the charges against her.

“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig said. The RICO charge “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
What the verdict changes for Huawei’s business is unclear. A U.S. jury has convicted Chinese technology giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and deceiving banks over its business in Iran, delivering a major victory for federal prosecutors after a years-long criminal case.

The verdict comes at a striking moment for a company Washington has spent years trying to contain. Despite U.S. restrictions that sharply curtailed Huawei's access to American technology, it has expanded into chipmaking and become an important player in China's artificial intelligence push, offering a domestic alternative to products from Nvidia.
What was Huawei found guilty of?
The government's case centered on allegations that Huawei systematically obtained technology from competitors while misleading banks and U.S. officials about business dealings in countries subject to American sanctions.
Prosecutors alleged a series of instances of technology theft. Those included claims that Huawei sold routers containing source code copied from Cisco Systems and that a worker removed part of a T-Mobile testing robot from a laboratory so it could be photographed and measured. Victim companies cited in court records also included Motorola Solutions, Quintel USA and Fujitsu.

She was accused of misleading HSBC about the company's Iran dealings but returned to China in 2021 after reaching a deferred prosecution agreement. The charges against her were later dropped.
From U.S. blacklist to Nvidia challenger
The U.S. placed Huawei on a trade blacklist in 2019, restricting its access to American technology amid longstanding national security concerns. Yet the measures have not removed the company from the global technology race.
Huawei continues to sell smartphones and telecommunications equipment internationally and has increasingly moved into semiconductors and AI infrastructure. Its expansion into chipmaking has made it an important Chinese alternative to companies such as Nvidia.
That competition has taken on added significance amid extraordinary turmoil at Nvidia, the American company that dominates the market for chips used to power advanced AI.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and longtime CEO, resigned on November 12 following revelations about extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a businesswoman whom U.S. officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The woman had been associated with a Singapore-based company scrutinized over whether advanced Nvidia chips were being diverted to China, although Reuters reported that it could not independently verify the intelligence allegation and China called it "groundless." Huang has not been accused of criminal wrongdoing.
Huang's departure proved short-lived. Nvidia's board reinstated him as president and CEO on Monday after receiving input from senior U.S. government officials and concluding that his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump, who publicly advocated for Huang's return, said he had pressed the company's board to reinstate him.
The reversal had an enormous market impact: Nvidia shares closed 31.5 percent higher Monday, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, though they did not recover all of the losses since Huang's resignation.
Huawei's growing role in the AI race
The turmoil at Nvidia comes as Washington and Beijing battle over access to advanced chips considered crucial to the development of AI.
The U.S. has restricted exports of advanced AI processors to China, while Huawei has become increasingly important to Beijing's push to develop domestic alternatives. Huawei's rise therefore adds another dimension to Tuesday's verdict: a company the U.S. prosecuted over allegations of stealing American technology has simultaneously developed into a significant player in China's effort to become less dependent on American suppliers.
The financial consequences of the verdict could still be substantial. Huawei could face billions of dollars in penalties, although the impact on a global business already largely shut out of the U.S. telecommunications market remains uncertain.

A federal jury found Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 criminal charges involving technology theft, financial fraud and sanctions violations, delivering a major verdict in a yearslong prosecution while acquitting the company of racketeering conspiracy.
Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei Technologies was convicted Tuesday, Nov. 24, on 10 federal criminal charges, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, following a two-month trial examining allegations that the company obtained proprietary American technology and misled financial institutions about its business dealings with Iran.
A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, returned the verdict against Huawei and its affiliates after hearing testimony concerning alleged technology theft, sanctions violations and financial transactions involving Iranian operations. The jury acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy, rejecting prosecutors’ allegation that Huawei operated as a coordinated criminal enterprise, as well as a separate obstruction conspiracy charge.
According to Reuters reporting on the verdict, the convictions followed more than two months of testimony involving over 60 prosecution witnesses and 15 defense witnesses. The case represents a significant outcome in a federal investigation that began in 2018 and has contributed to longstanding tensions between Washington and Beijing.
Huawei rejected the verdict, maintaining that the charges underlying its convictions lacked legal merit. The company said it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
The jury convicted Huawei on 10 of the 12 counts, including wire fraud, bank fraud, money laundering and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. The company also faced charges involving violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and efforts to defraud the United States.
Prosecutors argued that Huawei systematically obtained confidential technologies from American competitors and business partners over approximately two decades, using the information to advance its position in the global telecommunications equipment market.
The allegations involved proprietary technology belonging to several American companies, including Cisco Systems, T-Mobile, Quintel, CNEX and Fujitsu.
Federal prosecutors presented evidence that Huawei obtained or attempted to obtain information concerning wireless antennas, telecommunications equipment, semiconductor technology and other commercially valuable products.
One incident involved a T-Mobile testing robot used to evaluate smartphone performance. Jurors viewed surveillance footage that prosecutors said showed a Huawei employee removing part of the device and placing it in a backpack.
Another allegation concerned a Huawei engineer who entered a Fujitsu exhibition booth at a trade show and photographed equipment without authorization.
Prosecutors also alleged that Huawei improperly obtained Cisco router source code, sought access to Quintel antenna technology and used a university professor to acquire information concerning a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
The prosecution maintained that these incidents demonstrated a broader effort to acquire competitors’ proprietary information rather than isolated misconduct by individual employees.
Huawei’s attorneys disputed that characterization, arguing that prosecutors combined unrelated events into an exaggerated account of corporate wrongdoing.
During closing arguments, defense attorney Brian Heberlig accused the government of selecting a limited number of incidents to support allegations of a prolonged conspiracy.
He argued that Huawei’s success resulted from “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development,” rather than systematic theft of intellectual property.
The defense also challenged prosecutors’ allegations concerning Huawei’s financial dealings with Iran.
Federal authorities accused the company of misleading international banks, including HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas, about the extent of its Iranian operations.
Prosecutors maintained that Huawei concealed business relationships that exposed financial institutions to potential violations of American sanctions restricting transactions involving Iran.
The case centered partly on representations made to financial institutions concerning Skycom Tech, a company involved in Huawei’s Iranian business activities.
Prosecutors alleged that Huawei misrepresented its relationship with Skycom to reassure banks that transactions involving the company complied with U.S. sanctions.
The investigation gained international attention in December 2018 when Canadian authorities arrested Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver at the request of American prosecutors.
Meng, the daughter of Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei, was accused of misleading an HSBC executive about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom and its operations in Iran.
Her arrest triggered a diplomatic dispute involving China, Canada and the United States, with Beijing demanding her release.
Meng contested extradition for nearly three years before reaching a deferred prosecution agreement with American authorities in September 2021.
Under that arrangement, she acknowledged factual statements concerning misleading representations to a financial institution but did not enter a guilty plea. She subsequently returned to China, and the charges against her were later dismissed.
The agreement’s statement of facts became part of the evidence presented during Huawei’s criminal trial.
Prosecutors also called an HSBC banker who participated in a 2013 meeting with Meng to testify about representations concerning the company’s Iranian activities.
During closing arguments, federal prosecutor Meredith Arfa described how financial institutions began scrutinizing Huawei’s operations following media reporting about its business relationships.
“After the media started questioning Huawei’s operations in Iran, so did Huawei’s banks,” Arfa told jurors.
Huawei’s defense maintained that the banks were already aware of its Iranian operations and continued seeking the company’s business.
The verdict represents a significant legal development for a company that has faced extensive American restrictions over national security concerns.
In 2019, the Trump administration placed Huawei on the U.S. Commerce Department’s Entity List, imposing export licensing requirements that restricted the company’s access to American technology.
The restrictions complicated Huawei’s ability to obtain advanced semiconductors, software and other equipment used in telecommunications devices.
American officials have also raised concerns about potential security risks associated with Huawei’s telecommunications infrastructure, particularly equipment used in fifth-generation wireless networks.

In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September.

“No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but was heartened by the acquittals on racketeering conspiracy and another charge, conspiracy to obstruct justice. He called those not guilty verdicts “a vindication of the company and its good-faith compliance culture.”
“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hardworking company that we came to know and deeply respect,” Heberlig said outside the courthouse.

That hasn’t stopped the company from doing a robust business elsewhere. Its smartphones and other telecom equipment are sold globally. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors, becoming an important alternative in China to chips made by companies such as Nvidia.

“We remain focused on serving our customers and partners and ensuring continuous and stable business operations,” the statement said.

Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.

NEW YORK — A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday convicted Huawei on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, while acquitting the company of the government’s racketeering conspiracy charge.
The verdict followed closing arguments in which prosecutors portrayed the company’s alleged thefts, banking deceptions and efforts to obstruct investigators as coordinated actions serving its global business. Huawei’s defense argued that prosecutors had assembled isolated incidents into a false narrative of corporate criminality.
“Huawei violated our laws, empowered our enemies, and harmed our national security,” Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General M. Scott Proctor said after the verdict. “This conviction shows that the National Security Division and its partners will not rest until companies like Huawei are held to account for their bad conduct in an American court of justice.”
In a statement sent to The Bureau after the verdict, Huawei welcomed the racketeering acquittal and disputed the remaining charges.
“Today, a jury in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York acquitted Huawei of the government’s RICO charge.”
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” the statement says. “The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades.”
“We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
The competing interpretations of those earlier disputes had been central to the closing arguments. In his rebuttal, Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Pollack urged jurors to focus on the agreements underlying the conspiracy charges.
“Remember, a conspiracy is an agreement,” he said. “That’s the crime; the agreement itself.”
A day before the verdict, jurors sought guidance on the separate obstruction conspiracy charge, which prosecutors built partly on an intercepted call in which Huawei’s human resources and legal personnel discussed moving employees out of the United States.
On Monday, November 23, jurors asked whether Huawei had appeared pursuant to a subpoena in Washington and whether that investigation had transferred to the Eastern District of New York. Their note concerned Count 12, according to Inner City Press’s courtroom reporting.
The call followed the arrest of a Huawei employee who had worked on the company’s Iran business. The conduct underlying his arrest was withheld from the jury. But prosecutors argued that the company’s legal and human resources officials treated the arrest as a pretext for obtaining information about Huawei.
“What they did is they spoke completely dismissively of the arrest,” Pollack told jurors in his November 17 rebuttal.
Pollack said the call participants discussed getting other employees who had worked in sanctioned countries out of the United States immediately. He argued that their response revealed concern about investigators reaching the company’s evidence.
“Their first instinct is not to believe it, and to assume he wasn’t a rogue employee who did some crime on his own, but actually to assume that was all for show, and his arrest was really because the government was collecting evidence of Huawei’s crimes, so they need to get all of the evidence, out of the US and obstruct justice ASAP,” he said.
The human resources official, Pollack argued, was “clearly proposing a conspiracy to obstruct justice; clearly saying we need to get these people out of the country if they have information about our work in sensitive countries, absolutely.”
The defense argued that only one of the Huawei employees on the call had proposed removing employees and that the other never agreed.
Pollack said the defense had shown jurors “selective snippets” of the transcript. “I think you should read it,” he told them. “That lawyer does agree with it.”

He urged jurors “as enthusiastically as I can to read every word of that exhibit.”

The jury may have been convinced that Huawei is more than a criminal enterprise but stealing is clearly a big part of its path to success.
Huawei and its affiliates, prosecutors said, used “a pattern of racketeering activity” to steal trade secrets from American companies. The stolen information included source code and operating system manuals, according to an indictment. The company even launched a bonus program for employees who stole information from competitors, according to the indictment.
In one particularly brazen example of theft from 2004, prosecutors said, a Huawei employee was caught trying to steal from a competitor at a Chicago trade show. The employee, prosecutors said, was discovered late at night trying to photograph the inside of a networking device.
Other, similar incidents were testified to during the trial.
At trade shows, Huawei engineers would sneak photographs of other companies’ hardware, including their routers and internal circuitry, according to witness testimony. The second major element of the case involved Huawei's relationship with Skycom, a company that conducted business in Iran.
Prosecutors alleged that Huawei concealed the extent of its relationship with Skycom and misled financial institutions about transactions involving Iran.

Huawei Found Guilty Of Plotting To Steal US Trade Secrets And Lying To Banks Over Iran
A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets from American companies and bank fraud, closing out a case that began with the arrest of its chief financial officer in Canada nearly eight years ago.
The jury convicted Shenzhen-based Huawei Technologies and three affiliates of bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and money laundering, but acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy, the most serious charge and the one that cast Huawei as a criminal enterprise, according to Reuters and the AP.
Huawei headquarters building in Shenzhen (Cheng Xin / Getty Images)
Over a trial of more than two months that opened with jurors sworn in on Sept. 8, prosecutors called more than 60 witnesses and the defense 15; deliberations began on Nov. 18. As we reported when the trial opened, prosecutors told jurors that Huawei committed crimes over two decades, from stealing technology to lying to banks about Iran and then covering it up.
The trade secret charges, added in a superseding indictment in 2020, named Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu among the victims. Prosecutors said Huawei sold routers running source code copied from a competitor, photographed the circuitry of a rival's networking gear at a Chicago trade show, and took a robotic arm out of a competitor's lab to be photographed and measured. They also pointed to antenna technology from Quintel and a circuit board from CNEX.
The bank fraud counts go back to the original 2019 indictment. Prosecutors said Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business in Iran, passing off Skycom Tech, which the US says was an unofficial Huawei subsidiary, as an independent local partner. The company was also accused of doing business in North Korea and of lying to US officials.
Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei
"After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury. She said the company's top leaders set the tone and "engaged in criminal conduct."
Huawei's lawyers said investigators took isolated misconduct by a handful of its more than 200,000 employees and built it into a grand conspiracy. Defense attorney Brian Heberlig accused prosecutors of having "cherry-picked" incidents and of relying on "innuendo and facts ripped out of context," argued that the banks knew all about Huawei's Iran business and competed for it anyway, and said much of the supposedly stolen material was already public. He told jurors that Huawei pays billions in licensing fees, and 75% of that money goes to US companies.
The case's best-known defendant never saw a jury. Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's CFO and the founder's daughter, was arrested in Canada on a US warrant in December 2018 and fought extradition for nearly three years. She went home to China in 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement, in a swap that freed two Canadians Beijing had detained, and the US dropped the charges against her.
Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou
Brian Heberlig, Huawei’s lead lawyer, focused on the company’s acquittal on two charges, including the so-called RICO racketeering count, which he called the government’s lead charge. He said that the company would appeal the other counts.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig said. The RICO charge “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
What the verdict changes for Huawei's business is unclear. The company has been barred from selling equipment to US carriers for years, was put on the US trade blacklist in 2019, and has been shut out by Canada and Britain, and Beijing has called Washington's campaign against it "economic bullying." In the meantime Huawei has become China's main homegrown alternative to Nvidia's AI chips, and as a company it faces fines, not prison.

BROOKLYN (CN) — Jurors on Tuesday convicted Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei on 10 criminal counts, including bank fraud and wire fraud, along with conspiracies to steal trade secrets, violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and launder money.

Trial lasted for more than two months in the Eastern District of New York. Jury deliberations began shortly before 3 p.m. on Wednesday.
Prosecutors said their evidence encapsulated a culture of thievery at Huawei that went all the way to the top, accusing the company’s founder Ren Zhengfei of brushing off concerns about intellectual property theft and other top officials of offering employees bonuses for passing along confidential information from competing businesses.
Outside the courthouse, defense attorney Brian Heberlig called the RICO acquittal “a profound rejection of the United States’ narrative about what Huawei is.”
“As we maintained throughout the trial, that’s not the Huawei we knew or experienced. The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hardworking company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” said Heberlig, of the firm Steptoe LLP.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors in her Nov. 16 closing argument, which lasted about five hours, that Huawei built its empire on “theft, lies and cover-ups,” signaling to its employees, “You can lie and steal and cheat as long as you’re doing it for the benefit of Huawei.”
Jurors saw evidence of incidents involving U.S. companies including T-Mobile, Cisco Systems and Quintel. In one video shown to the jury, a Huawei employee, who had gained access to T-Mobile’s secure lab, snapped off a piece of a phone-testing robot called “Tappy,” which can simulate a human finger to use a touch screen device, and slipped it into his backpack.
In his closing argument, Heberlig said the government had put a “sinister spin” on ordinary business practices at Huawei, building its case from isolated incidents of employee misconduct.
Attorneys for Huawei, however, had to grapple with a 2021 deferred prosecution agreement signed by Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou, Ren’s daughter, who also goes by Kathy Meng.
Following her 2018 arrest in Vancouver, Canada, which strained relations between the U.S., its North American neighbor and China, Meng signed the agreement admitting to misleading HSBC executives about the company’s dealings in Iran.
The statements to HSBC and other banks include Huawei calling its subsidiary Skycom, which did business in Iran, a business partner, and claiming it had only limited operations in the sanctioned country.
According to the government, the company worked on networks that were used by the Iranian government to spy on citizens, including during 2009 demonstrations in Tehran.
Shortly before trial began in September, prosecutors announced they would not pursue two of the 14 counts against the Huawei defendants at trial, leaving jurors to determine the remaining 12 counts.
Heberlig said Huawei plans to appeal its convictions.
U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, a Barack Obama appointee, scheduled sentencing for September 2027. Huawei faces steep financial penalties. The company has been effectively banned since 2019 from selling its products in the U.S.
During a post-verdict discussion about deadlines, Heberlig said, “I don’t think ability to pay is going to be an issue here” and that Huawei has “more than sufficient” funds.
Huawei does business in more than 170 countries and holds more than 165,000 active patents for telecommunications, cloud, AI and device technology.
In a statement Tuesday, Huawei said it “takes its compliance obligations seriously.”
“We stand firmly committed to long-term investment in [research and development] and technological innovation for sound operations and sustainable growth,” Huawei said.

sources.text:
Chinese technology company Huawei was convicted in New York on seven federal counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and defrauding the United States.
The jury acquitted Huawei of two charges: racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.
Driving the news: The convictions followed accusations that Huawei stole technology from several American companies, abused the U.S. financial system, and supported the Iranian government in spying on its citizens.
- Prosecutors cited high-profile victims of Huawei’s alleged intellectual property theft, including Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA, and Fujitsu.
- The government argued that Huawei encouraged its 200,000 global employees to engage in deceptive and illegal practices to grow and protect the company’s business interests.
The other side: Huawei has rejected the charges as “without legal or factual merit,” welcomed the racketeering acquittal, and stated plans to appeal the conviction.
What we’re watching: Sentencing is scheduled for September 14, with Huawei potentially facing substantial fines and additional penalties.

sources.news_title: US Jury Convicts Huawei on Ten Counts but Clears It of Racketeering Conspiracy
sources.text:
US Jury Convicts Huawei on Ten Counts but Clears It of Racketeering Conspiracy
Huawei trial verdict: A federal jury in Brooklyn has convicted the Chinese telecoms group on ten criminal counts, including trade secret theft and bank fraud. Huawei and three subsidiaries had faced twelve counts, BILD reports. The jury acquitted the company of the most serious charge, racketeering conspiracy, which alleged that it operated as a criminal enterprise.
The trial lasted more than two months. Huawei could face heavy fines, but the sentence has not yet been determined.
Prosecutors accused Huawei of trying for years to steal technology from American firms, naming router software code from Cisco Systems, antenna technology from Quintel and semiconductor technology from CNEX.
Banks and the Iran link
The prosecution also said Huawei deceived banks including HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its ties to the firm Skycom in Iran. In her closing argument, prosecutor Meredith Arfa said: “After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig countered that prosecutors had “cherry-picked” individual incidents to build a conspiracy narrative. The US case began in 2018 with the arrest in Canada of chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, daughter of company founder Ren Zhengfei.

sources.news_title: Huawei is convicted on 10 of 12 counts in Brooklyn but cleared of racketeering
sources.text:
A US jury found Huawei guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets, but the racketeering charge, which prosecutors used to cast the whole company as a criminal enterprise, did not stick. If you buy or build on Huawei hardware, the split decides what comes next.
A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei Technologies on 10 of 12 counts on Tuesday, November 24, ending a criminal case that has run for nearly seven years. According to Bloomberg, the convictions cover conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering and violations of US sanctions law. The jury acquitted the company on racketeering conspiracy and on conspiracy to obstruct justice.
The trial ran about 11 weeks before US District Judge Ann Donnelly, and jurors deliberated for roughly four days. Huawei denied wrongdoing throughout. In a statement, the company welcomed the racketeering acquittal and said it disputes the remaining charges. No sentence or fine has been set.
The trade-secret evidence was strikingly small-scale for a case about one of the world's biggest telecom equipment makers. Jurors watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei employee removing part of T-Mobile's Tappy testing robot from a lab, and prosecutors argued the company built its business on repeated crimes.
Why the racketeering acquittal matters
Racketeering was the heaviest charge in the indictment the Justice Department announced when it first charged Huawei and its subsidiaries. It treated Huawei as a single enterprise run to commit crimes, the theory prosecutors use to reach an entire organization rather than individual acts. Jurors declined to accept it.
Huawei rotating chairman Xu Zhijun says US pressure helped China’s semiconductor industry grow faster. The bigger issue for investors is whether export controls are slowing China down or helping build a rival AI hardware stack. - how US chip controls accelerated China semiconductor development - Huawei says sanctions pushed China chipmaking faster forward
Frankly, that makes this a mixed result for Washington. The government proved that specific people at Huawei took things that weren't theirs and misled banks, but it didn't convince 12 jurors that the company as a whole existed to do it. That gap is where Huawei's lawyers will work.
Sentencing is still a way off. Reporting indicates that motions and responses ahead of it are set to start in the third week of January. Fines and any limits on how Huawei operates in the US are the numbers to watch.
The chip fight around the verdict
The timing is awkward for everyone. The verdict lands while Washington is tightening export rules on chips bound for China, and while Nvidia chief Jensen Huang faces scrutiny in Congress over China chip sales.
Don't over-read the link, though. This case is about conduct that largely dates from years ago, including the alleged Iran business that fed the sanctions and bank-fraud counts. A jury in Brooklyn didn't rule on Ascend AI chips, and nothing in the verdict itself restricts what Huawei sells today. Any new restriction would have to come from Commerce Department export controls or from the sentence Judge Donnelly eventually imposes.
For companies that do business in China, the practical lesson is narrower and more useful than the headlines. Prosecutors can build a trade-secret case from a single piece of borrowed test equipment, and a jury will accept it. If your staff handle partners' test equipment or visit rivals' labs, your compliance team should already be asking what they take away.
No post-trial motion or appeal has been filed or announced yet, and sentencing is still months away.

sources.news_title: Chinese tech giant Huawei is guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, US jury finds - The Business Journal Huawei convicted of trade secret conspiracy and bank fraud
sources.text:
A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge most often appears in organized crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to repeatedly poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners in the U.S. and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but was heartened by the acquittals on racketeering conspiracy and another charge, conspiracy to obstruct justice. He called those not guilty verdicts “a profound rejection of the United States’ narratives of what Huawei is” and “a vindication of the company and its good-faith compliance culture.”
“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hardworking company that we came to know and deeply respect,” Heberlig said outside court.
Huawei’s lawyers said U.S. investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn’t actually exist.
The company could face billions of dollars in penalties.
It’s unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
That hasn’t stopped the company from doing a robust business elsewhere. Its smartphones and other telecom equipment are sold globally. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors, becoming an important alternative in China to chips made by companies such as Nvidia.
The U.S. announced its criminal charges against Huawei in early 2019 and later expanded the allegations. The lengthy trial began in September.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.
The indictment against Huawei accused it of a long pattern of outright technology thefts. Huawei, prosecutors said, once sold internet routers containing source code copied from a competitor. In another episode, a person working for Huawei slipped into a competitor’s booth at a Chicago trade show to surreptitiously photograph the circuits inside another company’s networking device, the indictment said. Prosecutors said that on another occasion, a Huawei worker removed a robotic arm from a competitor’s lab so it could be photographed and measured.
The victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to court records.
“The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating U.S. sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury at the trial.
In his closing argument to jurors, Huawei’s lawyer said prosecutors leaned on “innuendo and facts ripped out of context,” and testimony from ex-employees “with a bone to pick,” to pursue a company that had relied on “hard work, innovation and competition” to succeed.
“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” Heberlig said, noting that much of the material the U.S. alleges was stolen was already public.
“You can’t steal a secret that isn’t a secret,” he said.
He said Huawei paid billions of dollars in licensing fees over the years, with 75% of that money going to U.S. companies, and had reprimanded or fired employees found to have engaged in wrongdoing.
Heberlig noted that lines of Cisco source code turned up in Huawei software more than two decades ago. He said when the source-code copying was discovered, Huawei recalled routers sold in the U.S. and offered to replace them with Cisco routers and created a “compliance culture that permeates Huawei today.”
No individual executives or employees faced trial, although prosecutors at one point also brought criminal charges against Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou. They accused her of misleading HSBC bank about the company’s business dealings in Iran.
Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, was arrested in Canada in 2018, but ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its case against Meng.
The trial in New York overlapped with a summit meeting between President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the technology-centric city of Shenzhen, China.
